standard.title: Science communication shapes policy
standard.description: explore the role of science communication in informing individual viewpoints and community policies and regulations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can investigate how individuals and communities use scientific knowledge to identify problems and make decisions (AC9S5H02). They have not yet explored how the communication of science — not just the knowledge itself — shapes viewpoints and drives policy.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore the role of science communication in informing individual viewpoints and community policies and regulations.

nodes.label: Science communication takes many forms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different forms of science communication and recognise that how science is communicated affects what people understand
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two forms of science communication (e.g. media reports, scientific publications, public campaigns); explain how each reaches a different audience
nodes.typical_width: Compare how the same scientific finding is communicated differently for different audiences; explain what is emphasised, simplified or omitted in each
wider: Reflect on the role of contemporary First Nations Australians scientists, such as Wiradjuri astrophysicist Kirsten Banks, in communicating science to diverse audiences
Compare how a scientific finding was communicated in a peer-reviewed journal vs a news article vs social media — what changes and why?
Investigate how science communicators choose what to include and exclude and how this shapes public understanding

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of communication forms — journals, news, social media, public campaigns, two-way Indigenous knowledge communication — to see that the form-audience-content relationship is general, not specific to one medium. Each form in the repertoire demonstrates a different set of communication choices and trade-offs.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Kirsten Banks as a First Nations science communicator is rich beyond the minimum — she represents a two-way communication model where Indigenous astronomical knowledge and Western astronomy are communicated together to diverse audiences. This direction connects to AC9S7H02 and gives advancing students a contemporary case of science communication that challenges the default Western-scientist-to-public model.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two forms of science communication
Explains how each form reaches a different audience
Recognises that communication choices affect what people understand

nodes.label: Communication informs individual viewpoints
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication informs and changes individual viewpoints on science-related issues
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example where science communication changed individual viewpoints on an issue; explain what was communicated and how viewpoints changed
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how science communication about two different issues (e.g. conservation, waste) informed individual viewpoints; explain the mechanisms by which communication influenced understanding
wider: Explore how Dame Jane Goodall's communication of her research changed individual viewpoints about primate conservation
Investigate how science communication about waste materials changed individual behaviour around household waste
Analyse how science communication can both inform and misinform — compare an effective and an ineffective example

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'communication' with 'the science itself' — treating viewpoint change as automatic once knowledge exists, rather than understanding that how science is communicated determines whether and how viewpoints shift. Seeing multiple examples where the same knowledge was communicated differently with different viewpoint outcomes (Goodall, waste communication) helps resolve this conflation.

success_criteria: Names a specific example where science communication changed viewpoints
Explains what was communicated and how viewpoints changed
Distinguishes the role of communication from the knowledge itself

nodes.label: Communication shapes community policies and regulations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication leads to changes in community policies and regulations
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example where science communication led to a policy or regulation change; explain the connection between the communication and the policy outcome
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how science communication across two contexts led to specific policy or regulation changes; explain the pathway from communication to policy
wider: Examine how science communication of endangered species has led to fishing catch and hunting limits
Examine how global reporting on high-impact weather events has led to warning systems and evacuation policies
Investigate how First Nations Australians are using two-way approaches such as Caring for Country initiatives to influence policies

response_modes.reason: Students commonly name a policy change without tracing the pathway from communication to policy outcome — they establish correlation (communication happened, policy changed) without explaining the causal mechanism. Scaffolding the reasoning explicitly (what was communicated, to whom, through what channels, and how did this reach policy makers?) is what moves students from correlation to explanation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Caring for Country direction is rich — it represents a two-way policy influence model where First Nations communities are active communicators shaping policy, not just recipients of science communication. This challenges the default science-to-policy communication model and connects to AC9S7H02. Advancing students who investigate this case gain a more complete picture of how science communication operates in Australian policy contexts.
success_criteria: Names a specific example where science communication led to a policy or regulation change
Explains the pathway from communication to policy outcome
Distinguishes the policy change from the underlying scientific knowledge

nodes.label: The role of science communication in society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication plays an ongoing role in informing viewpoints and shaping policies across different contexts
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how science communication informed viewpoints and shaped policy in one case, connecting communication choices to outcomes
nodes.typical_width: Compare two cases where science communication had different impacts — one primarily on viewpoints, one primarily on policy — and explain what made each effective
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of a science communication campaign — what worked, what didn't, and what could be improved?
Investigate how science communication of the impact of waste materials led to both changed viewpoints and community recycling policies
Construct an argument about what makes science communication effective at driving both viewpoint change and policy change

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the communication forms thread (Node 1), the viewpoints thread (Node 2), and the policy thread (Node 3) into a coordinated account of science communication's role in society. Students who can address each separately but cannot connect them into a coherent explanation of how communication choices produce viewpoint and policy outcomes have not met the descriptor's exploratory demand.

The effectiveness evaluation direction — what made communication work or not work — requires explicit criteria scaffolding. Students need support in identifying what 'effective' means across the viewpoint and policy dimensions, not just narrating what happened. Without this scaffold, evaluations default to impressionistic judgements.

success_criteria: Explains how communication choices connected to both viewpoint and policy outcomes
Identifies what made the communication effective or ineffective
